extracted.intended_audience: novelists preparing agent submission packages / writers querying literary agents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing a professional novel synopsis to include in an agent submission pack; explains structure, length, tone, presentation, and common mistakes with examples and a model synopsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synopsis scope / completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: A short summary of your story, in its entirety, from beginning to end — 'soup to nuts, nose to tail.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every major character, any big turning point or climactic scene, and all plot twists should get a mention; the synopsis must give the full rundown of the book's story (unlike a blurb) so agents can see the whole narrative arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral, business-like tone (not salesy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Written in fairly neutral, non-salesy language; a synopsis is a business document, not the novel itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be clear and to the point; 'tell' rather than 'show'; avoid jacket-blurb language or overt marketing copy — aim for a slightly dry, professional voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the novel's structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The synopsis should follow the same broad structure as your novel; your novel's structure trumps any chronological issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the book has two intertwining time-strands, present events in the order they appear in the novel rather than re-chronologising them for the synopsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length: ~500–800 words (check agents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Synopses are probably about 500–800 words in length, though agents' requirements differ and you should check each agent's submission guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many good synopses run to two nicely formatted pages (reasonable line spacing, normal margins, sensible font). Don’t assume one-page maximum unless the agent explicitly requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person and tense: third person, present tense
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the synopsis in the third person and the present tense, even if the novel is narrated in first person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: instead of 'I am a police constable...', use 'Fiona Griffiths is a police constable...'; present tense keeps the agent feeling connected to events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Be well-presented with no typos or spelling mistakes; use normal fonts, normal margins, and line spacing no narrower than 1.5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep formatting professional and readable; controlled spacing and ordinary fonts help agents read quickly. Most agents expect a tidy, standard document.

rubrics_metrics.name: File naming conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use generic filenames like 'synopsis.doc'; use a filename that helps the agent identify the work, e.g. title-synopsis.doc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: farewell-to-arms-synopsis.doc — helps an agent who may receive many similar files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight main character names on first introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Put the names of main characters in bold or CAPS when you first introduce them to make the synopsis easier to navigate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This visual cue helps agents scan the document; do this consistently for primary characters only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character thumbnails / quick identifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a swift resume of who main characters are on first introduction (e.g., 'James Bond, (38), a British agent — handsome, cruel, seductive...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may insert ages in brackets; keep thumbnails short and functional — focus on role/traits that matter to the plot and character arc rather than long biography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layer in character emotion and arcs
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond plot mechanics, include who characters are and how the events of the story impact them — layer in emotional/character-type language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate space to show why the plot matters to characters (the article suggests ~200 words for character/emotion), so the synopsis doesn't read as cold plot machinery. Example contrast given from Twilight shows small emotional phrasing makes the text more engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional top-line hook or 2–3 line sell
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can concisely 'sell' the story in 2–3 compelling lines, you may insert that snippet at the top of the synopsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep it short and factual; this is optional but can quickly signal the premise to an agent before they read the full synopsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure your synopsis using narrative beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Build the synopsis from structure headings: Status quo; Inciting incident; Rising action/Developments; Crisis; Resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't try to compress the full manuscript into a precis; instead sketch your plot around these beats (about 300 words for the structure) and then layer character material on top.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-count allocation between plot and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with ~300 words to outline the structure/plot beats and use the remaining ~200 words to layer in character information and emotional stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within the plot section, 'developments' will often be the largest portion (maybe 40–50% of your synopsis word count). Missing excessive detail is intentional — omit fine subplots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal major plot points and spoilers
rubrics_metrics.description: A synopsis is the 'ultimate plot spoiler' — include all major plot points, twists, and the ending; do not hide the plot twist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents expect the full trajectory, including how the story resolves; hiding the ending is counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be selective: omit subplots and avoid over-detail
rubrics_metrics.description: You may skip subplots or finer details; avoid going into extensive setting description or unnecessary minutiae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give only what is necessary to understand the main arc (example: for Austen-style setting, a single short phrase will suffice). Agents understand a synopsis is an approximation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit number of named characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the number of character names small — four or five is a maximum an agent wants to deal with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If other characters must be referenced, use functional labels like 'the CIA agent' or 'the beautiful doctor' rather than naming many minor players.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid meta-telling and weak framing phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't write meta lines like 'Then the novel picks up the story of Kate and Jacob...' — state the events directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin sentences with the action/characters (e.g., 'Meanwhile, Kate and Jacob...') to keep the synopsis immediate and clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stick to each agent's specified word count and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agent specifies a particular word count, aim to meet it; you may need several versions of your synopsis to match different agents' guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to adhere to stated requirements is a common rejection trigger; prepare different-length synopses if querying multiple agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation/content pitfalls to avoid (common mistakes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of frequent errors: missing the agent's word count by a mile; going into setting detail; over-describing characters; hiding plot twists; starting with meta-framing; cramming in too many names; forgetting to put character names in CAPS or bold; omitting the title; using an unhelpful filename; poor writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be scrupulous about these issues: include title and author at top, use appropriate filename, use CAPS/bold on first mention of names, keep prose tidy and functional, and follow agent instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: make the agent request the manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: The synopsis's job is to outline your plot and demonstrate a clear story arc and satisfying ending so an agent will ask to see the full manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It should tell an agent directly and clearly what your plot is, identify main characters and their arcs, state the hook/premise, demonstrate appeal and rising momentum, and share a satisfying ending.
